tail/dist: Back to “I fed my”, and the model's probabilities for the next token, most likely first: cat, dog and fish, then sofa, ran and blue, which make no sense here.
tail/tail: Sorted like this, the bars trail off into a long, thin end, called the tail. Each token in it is unlikely, but together they add up: zero point two here.
tail/dart: Lay the bars end to end and throw darts, as sampling does, and one throw in five lands in the tail: I fed my sofa.
tail/stuck: And the mistake stays. The model reads “I fed my sofa” as the text so far, and builds every later word on it.
tail/holtzman: In 2019, Ari Holtzman and colleagues, who found greedy text bland, found sampled text incoherent: almost unrelated to what came before.
tail/blame: They blamed the unreliable tail: in a real model, tens of thousands of unlikely tokens that together get far too many picks.
topk/cut: So cut the tail off before sampling. The simplest cut keeps a fixed number, k, of the most likely tokens, and drops the rest.
topk/fan: In 2018, Angela Fan, Mike Lewis and Yann Dauphin wrote stories this way, picking each word from only the ten most likely. It is called top-k sampling.
topk/kept: Here, with k of three, cat, dog and fish stay. But together they hold only zero point eight of the probability, not one.
topk/renorm: So divide each by zero point eight. Cat's zero point four becomes one half.
topk/name: Dog and fish become zero point three one and zero point one nine, and the three add up to one again. That rescaling is called renormalizing, and sampling picks among them.
nucleus/context: But how many tokens make sense depends on the text so far, called the context. After “Once upon a”, the model is sure: time holds zero point eight five.
nucleus/flat: After “My favorite color is”, it is unsure: the probability spreads over many colors.
nucleus/fixed: No fixed k suits both. A k of three keeps two junk tokens after once upon a, and cuts good colors after the other.
nucleus/topp: So Holtzman's team, in their 2019 paper, proposed keeping the fewest most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, a number such as zero point eight. This is top-p sampling.
nucleus/add: On “I fed my”, add from the top: cat alone is zero point four, and with dog, zero point six five.
nucleus/reach: With fish, the total reaches zero point eight, and exactly p counts. So top-p keeps three, and renormalizes them as top-k did.
nucleus/adapt: After once upon a, time alone passes p: top-p keeps one token. After my favorite color is, five. The kept set grows and shrinks with how sure the model is.
nucleus/nucleus: They called that set the nucleus: a small core that holds most of the probability, as an atom's nucleus holds most of its mass. Top-p is also called nucleus sampling.
ends/one: Turn either dial all the way down. With k of one, or a tiny p, only the top token is kept. Renormalized, it gets probability one: greedy decoding.
ends/all: Turn them all the way up: k equal to V, the vocabulary size, or a p of one, which only the whole vocabulary reaches. Nothing is cut: plain sampling again.
ends/order: Neither dial ever flattens the bars, as a high temperature does. They only cut, and what survives keeps its order and its proportions.
